alerts.title: Rising creatinine and declining eGFR on TDF
alerts.message: Guidelines note that in patients on TDF, intercurrent illnesses with dehydration or sepsis may cause renal function deterioration, and creatinine (eGFR) should be checked. This patient's creatinine has steadily risen from 0.9 mg/dL (2020) to 1.4 mg/dL (2026), with eGFR now 52 mL/min/1.73m². TDF is a known cause of proximal tubular toxicity and progressive renal impairment. Evidence supporting drug attribution: the gradual decline parallels 3 years of TDF exposure, and urinalysis shows proteinuria (1+), consistent with tubular dysfunction. Evidence against: the patient has no oedema or hypertension, and occasional ibuprofen use (2–3×/week) may also contribute to renal injury. The progressive trend over 6 years is concerning even though the latest value alone is not yet critical.

evidence.recommended_action: Evaluate renal function trends; consider TDF substitution if tubular toxicity confirmed. Assess for alternative causes of proteinuria. Reduce or discontinue ibuprofen. Refer for nephrology evaluation if proteinuria persists.

alerts.title: No clinician assessment or plan documented
alerts.message: No assessment or plan has been documented for this visit despite abnormal renal findings. The patient has a progressively rising creatinine, reduced eGFR (52), and proteinuria on urinalysis, all of which require clinical evaluation and a management plan. Guidelines indicate that renal function monitoring in patients on TDF is important, particularly when intercurrent illness is present. The absence of any documented plan represents a significant gap in care for a patient with evidence of potential TDF nephrotoxicity. Additionally, no monitoring orders for follow-up renal function or urinalysis have been placed.

evidence.recommended_action: Document assessment addressing the creatinine trend, eGFR, and proteinuria. Outline a management plan including renal monitoring interval, ibuprofen counselling, and consideration of TDF substitution if indicated.

alerts.title: Ibuprofen use with renal impairment on TDF
alerts.message: The patient takes ibuprofen 400 mg two to three times weekly for headaches, concurrent with TDF therapy and declining renal function (eGFR 52, creatinine 1.4). NSAIDs can reduce renal perfusion via prostaglandin inhibition and may accelerate kidney injury, particularly in patients with pre-existing renal impairment. TDF itself is nephrotoxic, and the combination of TDF with regular NSAID use compounds the risk of further renal decline. The proteinuria (1+) may reflect ongoing tubular damage from TDF, which ibuprofen could exacerbate. Discontinuing or minimising ibuprofen is an immediately modifiable risk factor.

evidence.recommended_action: Counsel patient to discontinue or minimise ibuprofen use. Recommend alternative headache management such as paracetamol. Monitor renal function after ibuprofen cessation to assess for stabilisation or improvement.

alerts.title: Viral load monitoring frequency may be reduced
alerts.message: Guidelines state that for patients on DTG-based first-line ART with viral load <50 copies/mL for more than 1 year and reliable adherence, monitoring frequency can be reduced from every 6 months to every 12 months. This patient has viral load <50 copies/mL, CD4 of 584, and adherence consistently >95% by pill count over 3 years on TLD. If these criteria are met, the next viral load could be scheduled at 12 months rather than 6, reducing patient burden. This is an optimisation opportunity rather than a safety concern.

evidence.recommended_action: If VL has been <50 copies/mL for >1 year with reliable adherence, extend VL monitoring interval to 12 months per guideline recommendations.
